notes:
I've written notes on Psalm 102 from about a dozen commentaries. I could only search and fetch a limited number of pages, so some verses have more notes than others.

**What's missing:**
- The Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 23, so I have Guzik on vv. 24–27 only from search snippets.
- I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, catholic.com, or the Lutheran and Pentecostal-specific sites.
- I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so there's no section on them.
- The pages don't present their differences as disputes between denominations. Where I name a tradition, I've used the label you gave each site, or the label on the page.

## Introduction and title

- **Who wrote it and when.** Guzik notes Jerusalem is pictured in ruins. If that ruin is literal, the psalm may come from the exile; Adam Clarke followed this thinking and suggested the author could be Daniel, Jeremiah, or Nehemiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- **An older critical view.** Ellicott says the psalm has no repentance and no idea of vicarious suffering. For this reason many critics bring the psalm down to the Antiochean period, when Jerusalem suffered so much. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-102.html
- **Point of difference: is it a "penitential" psalm?**
  - *For:* Guzik says traditional Christian liturgy counts it among the seven penitential psalms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/ Benson calls it the fifth of those Psalms styled Penitential. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-1.htm GotQuestions says that in these psalms the writer admits his wrongdoing and asks forgiveness. https://www.gotquestions.org/penitential-psalms.html
  - *Against:* Spurgeon (Baptist) says It is scarcely correct to call it a penitential Psalm, for the sorrow of it is rather of one suffering than sinning. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps102.cfm Coffman cites Kidner that it has been "miscalled" penitential, since it confesses no sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html
- **Point of difference: how much of the psalm is about Christ?** Kidner (cited by Coffman) treats the whole psalm as Messianic. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html Matthew Henry says that because Hebrews applies vv. 25–26 to Christ, the psalm speaks either of his affliction or of the afflictions of his church for his sake. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_102.cfm

## Verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- The title says this is a prayer for anyone afflicted. Henry: Here is a prayer put into the hands of the afflicted; let them present it to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-1.htm
- Spurgeon says the sufferer grieves more for Zion and the house of the Lord, than for his own house. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps102.cfm
- Catholic: Augustine says the repeated request ("hear my prayer… let my cry come") shows how intensely he is praying. He then reads the psalm as Christ speaking, asking when the Father ever turned His face from the Son. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801102.htm

**v. 2:** Guzik: the suffering was bad, but feeling that God did not see or care made it far worse. When the psalmist sensed God's favour, he could bear it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/

**v. 3:**
- "Like smoke" means his days pass in obscurity, and swiftly, and irrecoverably (Benson). Another reading he mentions: grief has dried him out the way smoke dries things hung in it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-1.htm
- The Treasury of David notes the same phrase is used of God's enemies in Ps 37:20. The righteous sufferer is complaining that he is getting the fate of the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-102.html
- Catholic: Augustine links smoke with pride, which swells and then vanishes. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801102.htm

**v. 4:** Guzik, quoting Horne: grief and fasting go together. Ahab, David and Daniel all lost the will to eat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/

**v. 5:**
- Guzik compares Job 19:20: he is so thin there seems to be nothing between bone and skin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Coffman says no disease known to ancient or modern doctors fits all these symptoms, so the passage may be figurative. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 6:**
- The birds are emblems of loneliness and gloom. Guzik quotes Poole that the "pelican" may be the bittern, a solitary, mournful bird. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Coffman quotes a traveller, Dr. Thompson, describing the pelican as a picture of melancholy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html
- Catholic: Augustine reads the three birds and their three places (wilderness, ruins, housetop) as symbols. Of the pelican he says I suppose that Christ born of a Virgin is here meant. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801102.htm

**v. 7:** Guzik quotes Poole that the Hebrew word for "sparrow" can mean any bird that sits alone keeping watch on the rooftops. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/

**v. 8:**
- Constable: his enemies used him as their example of a man God had cursed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/102-8.html
- Guzik quotes Horne: people's mockery is often the bitterest part of God's discipline. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/

**v. 9:**
- Constable thinks the mourning ashes he put on his head had fallen into his food. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/102-8.html
- Constable also says the ashes and tears may simply be figures for grief. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 10:**
- "Lifted me up and cast me away": Spurgeon's image is a wrestler who lifts his opponent only to throw him down harder. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Coffman: this verse is the only hint of sin in the psalm. If it describes the exile, the sin may be the nation's rather than the sufferer's own. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 11:** Guzik quotes Horne: a shadow keeps lengthening until it vanishes into darkness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/ Henry: the psalmist saw himself as a dying man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-1.htm

**v. 12:**
- Turning point. Up to v. 11 the psalm is full of "I", "me" and "my"; with "But You" the focus moves to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Constable: the "You" is emphatic in the Hebrew, sharpening the contrast with the psalmist's short life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 13:**
- If the psalm is from the exile, the "set time" is the 70 years set by God for Israel's captivity (Jeremiah 25:11-13 and 29:10). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-102.cfm
- Coffman agrees that the psalmist was remembering Jeremiah's promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 14:**
- Even in his own misery the psalmist cares about his community and loves even the ruins. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: by analogy, the weakest church member should be precious to us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Constable: the godly in Israel grieved over Zion's ruined state. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 15:**
- Guzik: God's restoring Jerusalem is the first stage of a wider work among the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Coffman goes further: from this verse on the subject becomes the Kingdom of the Messiah, since only then would the Gentiles fear the LORD. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 16:** Coffman reads the rebuilding of Zion as the founding of Christ's Church (Acts 15:16), and God appearing in glory as Christ's first coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 17:**
- Spurgeon (in Guzik): the "destitute" are the poor left among the ruins and the captives far away. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Henry: this is written down so that no one despairs if their prayers are not answered at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/102-17.html

**v. 18:** Readings of "a people not yet created":
- **Future generations.** Barnes: each new generation is a real "creation". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-18.htm
- **The church rising again.** Calvin: the return from exile was like a second birth. Let no desolation take away the hope that God brings the Church forth from the darkness of death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/102-18.html
- **New creatures in Christ.** Gill (Baptist): either people born when this happens, or people who shall become new creatures; be created in Christ Jesus. Clarke cites the Syriac title, which takes it to mean Gentiles converted through Christ. Same page.
- **Simply a record.** Wesley's note says only that this great deliverance will be carefully recorded. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-102.html
- **Other notes.** Ellicott: this is the only place in the Psalms where the memory of events is said to be kept in writing. Pulpit says Ezra and Nehemiah made that record. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-18.htm

**vv. 19–20:**
- Guzik pictures God bending down to see, to hear and to act. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- Cambridge (via Biblehub): Israel in exile is compared to a condemned captive languishing in prison. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-20.htm
- Coffman applies the verses to Christ's ministry (Luke 4:18): the prisoners are captives of sin, and the death is eternal death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html

**vv. 21–22:** Coffman: these will happen when the Gentiles are gathered in, which only "the current dispensation" of grace fits. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html

**v. 23:**
- Guzik: the psalm now returns to the writer's weakness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-102.cfm
- Gill: God, not an enemy, weakened him. He offers several possible applications: the returning exiles, the church waiting for the Messiah, or saints waiting for the glory of the last days. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/psalms/102-23.html
- **Septuagint (Greek) wording.** Brenton's translation reads He answered him in the way of his strength: tell me the fewness of my days. https://www.blueletterbible.org/bes/psa/102/1/ Coffman says this wording makes God the speaker. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html
- Catholic: Augustine, working from the Greek-based Latin, reads "she" (the Church) as answering God in unity. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801102.htm

**v. 24:** Catholic: Augustine takes this as the Church asking to last until the end of the world, against heretics who said she had died out. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801102.htm

**vv. 25–27 (the main point of difference: Hebrews 1:10–12):**
- **The usual Christ-centred reading.** Guzik says Hebrews quotes these verses as the Father's words to the Son. In the Hebrew they are spoken to Yahweh; the Septuagint, which Hebrews quotes, makes it clearer that God is speaking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
- **Kidner (via Coffman).** The Septuagint of vv. 23f shows the Father answering the Son, which implies the sufferer in the whole psalm is the incarnate Son. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-102.html
- **Gill.** These verses prove Christ's deity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/102-25.htm
- **A more cautious view.** Ellicott admits the difficulty that the words in the psalm would appear to be directly addressed to God as Creator. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hebrews-1.html The Expositor's Greek Testament quotes F. F. Bruce: either the writer of Hebrews saw creation as the pre-existent Christ's work, or he gave Christ that role because of texts like this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/1-10.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed).** The point is human frailty: we come before God bringing nothing but our emptiness. The Church is exempt from passing away because God's word is her foundation. https://www.ccel.org/study/Ps_102:25-102:28
- **v. 26 detail.** Ellicott: the words for "garment" and "vesture" both refer to the outer cloak Jews wore. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-102.html

**v. 28 (point of difference: who are "the children"?):**
- **Calvin (Reformed).** God's servants are made secure by their union with God, not the way the world is held together. The "seed" means only descendants who keep their parents' faith, not every physical descendant. https://www.ccel.org/study/Ps_102:25-102:28
- **Wesley (Methodist).** Even if heaven and earth perish, our children will be happily restored to, and settled in, their own land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-102.html
- **Guzik's summary.** The writer does not expect rescue in his own lifetime. He trusts that God's promises will be kept for generations to come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-102/
